newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Japan plutonium shipment raises New Zealand fears.
newsitem.headline: Japan plutonium shipment raises New Zealand fears.

text.p: New Zealand has expressed strong concern to Tokyo about the planned route of a ship carrying processed nuclear waste from France to Japan, Foreign Minister Don McKinnon said on Tuesday.
"What we want the Japanese to know is that we are concerned about the movement of the ship," McKinnon said.
He said other South Pacific nations were also protesting over the British freighter Pacific Teal, which left the French Channel port of Cherbourg on Monday.
The ship's route has been kept secret and McKinnon said New Zealand, a self-declared nuclear-free zone, would decide on what further action to take once the route was known.

Environmental group Greenpeace said a French diplomatic cable leaked in December indicated the ship would travel around the Cape of Good Hope, through the Tasman Sea between New Zealand and Australia and then north through the Pacific Ocean.

"We haven't had confirmation whether it is going to go through the Tasman Sea," McKinnon said. "Legally it can go through the Tasman Sea, (but) we certainly do not want it inside our 200 mile economic zone, let alone territorial waters."
The government could not legally try to stop the shipment unless it passed through New Zealand's territorial waters, which extend 12 miles (19 kilometres) from the shore, McKinnon said.
"The dangers of the deadly plutonium trade will directly threaten our region when this shipment of 'plutonium waste' passes though the Tasman," Greenpeace said in a statement.
The waste initially came from Japan and was processed at La Hague under a deal between the French state company COGEMA (Compagnie generale des matieres nucleaires) and 10 Japanese power companies.
Greenpeace, which is protesting at the secrecy surrounding such shipments, said it expected 3,000 cargoes of plutonium waste to be moved over the next 10 to 15 years.
